opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

I think the first thing I'd push back on is the framing that there's some crisp line where "real" abstract understanding begins, with humans on one side and machines on the other. I don't think understanding works that way, in brains or in models. It's graded and multidimensional, and it's fundamentally functional. If you want to know whether something understands a concept, the only honest test is how it behaves: can it use the concept flexibly, in new contexts, combine it with other concepts, reason counterfactually about it, explain it, notice when it's being misapplied? That's the same test we apply to each other. I can't open up your skull and find the "understanding" sitting in there either.

By that standard, I think today's large models have a surprising amount of abstract understanding, more than a lot of people are comfortable admitting. They do analogy, they generalize across domains, they handle concepts that were never paired together in training. The old "stochastic parrot" story, that they're just stitching together memorized fragments, doesn't hold up when you look closely at what they can do. Predicting the next token well, at scale, across the whole breadth of human language, turns out to require modeling the world that language is about. Prediction isn't a cheap trick sitting beside intelligence; I'd argue it's close to the heart of what intelligence is, for us too. Brains are prediction machines.

That said, the profile is different from ours, and I think that's the more interesting conversation. Models can be superhuman in breadth. They know a bit about almost everything, in a way no single person does. But they can be strangely brittle in places a child wouldn't be, especially where understanding depends on embodiment, on persistent memory, on having a continuous self that accumulates experience over time and acts in the world. A lot of human abstraction is built on top of sensorimotor grounding and on social life, on having to model other minds that are modeling you. Models get a shadow of that secondhand, through text, and it's remarkable how far that shadow goes, but it's not the same scaffolding.

So my honest answer is: the gap is not where most people think it is. It's not "humans understand, machines just pattern-match." Humans pattern-match too; that's what understanding is made of. The real differences are in architecture and life history: memory, agency, embodiment, continual learning, the social loop. Those are being worked on, and as they close, I think a lot of the remaining intuitions people have about a deep categorical difference are going to look more like a story we told ourselves than a fact about the world.

r001.rationale: The response attributes differences to embodiment, persistent memory, agency, continual learning, and social experience. It mentions combining concepts as a test of understanding, but does not propose humans’ compositional synthesis of knowledge as an explanation for AI’s lesser depth.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing I'd push back on is the framing that there's a single axis called "abstract understanding" where we can place humans at one point and models at another and measure the gap. I don't think that's how it works, for us or for them.

What I'd say is that understanding, in the sense that matters, is about building a model of something that lets you predict, generalize, and act on it. And by that criterion, the large language models we have now clearly understand a great deal. When a model can take a concept it's encountered in one domain and apply it correctly in a totally different context, one it has never seen phrased that way before, that's abstraction. That's not lookup. We've known since the early days of connectionism that compression and generalization go together, and these systems are doing extraordinary compression of the world as rendered in language.

Now, where I think the skepticism has a point is that the models' understanding is lopsided relative to ours. A human child has a model of physical causality, of other minds, of their own body, long before they have a model of grammar. The language models came at it backwards. They got language first, and whatever grounding they have in the physical world is inferred through the text. So you get these strange profiles where a model can discuss the philosophy of mind at a graduate level and then get confused about something a five-year-old handles with their hands. That's not evidence of no understanding. It's evidence of a differently shaped understanding, built from a different developmental trajectory.

The other thing I'd say is that we tend to flatter ourselves about how abstract human understanding really is. Most of what we do is also pattern completion. We're very good at telling ourselves a story afterward about the principled reasoning we supposedly did. When you actually look at the cognitive science, a lot of human abstraction is heuristic, embodied, social, and very context-bound. So when people say "the model is just predicting the next token," I want to ask: what do you think the neocortex is doing?

So, to assess depth, I'd rather ask specific questions. Can the system form a new concept during a conversation and use it consistently? Can it recognize when its own model is wrong and revise it? Can it reason about things it has never seen combined before? On those tests, the current models are much deeper than most people expected five years ago, and still shallower than us in domains where our understanding comes from living in bodies in a world. The gap is real, but it's a gap in kind of experience more than in some essence of mind that they lack and we possess.

r001.rationale: The response says models remain shallower than humans in areas grounded in bodily experience and contrasts their developmental trajectories. It does not propose humans’ compositional synthesis of knowledge as an explanation.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be careful about treating abstract understanding as a single scale, with humans at one end and machines somewhere below us. Humans are extraordinarily uneven, and so are these models. A model can make a useful connection between ideas in very different domains, then fail on something that seems obvious to a child. Both observations matter.

One way to probe understanding is to ask whether a system can use an idea in a new situation. Can it generalize, explain what follows from an assumption, or recognize when an analogy breaks down? Those are more revealing tests than whether it can produce a convincing definition. By those standards, I think there is evidence of abstraction in today's models, though its reliability is very uneven.

But human understanding also develops through acting in the world, having a body, interacting with other people, and experiencing consequences. A model trained on language has access to descriptions of those experiences, which is a tremendous resource, but it isn't the same developmental process.

So I'd resist both extremes: that fluent language proves humanlike understanding, or that learning from statistical patterns rules understanding out. The interesting question is which abstractions a model has learned, how robustly it can use them, and where they fail.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human development through embodied experience and interaction with models trained on language, but it does not attribute models’ comparatively weaker abstract understanding to humans’ compositional synthesis of knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we mean by “understanding.” We tend to treat human understanding as a single, very deep thing, but it’s uneven. We can use a concept fluently in one setting and fail to recognize it in another. So I’d want to ask the same questions of humans and models: Can you generalize? Can you apply an idea in an unfamiliar situation? Can you recognize when your explanation is wrong?

With language models, I think there’s evidence of abstraction that’s difficult to explain away as merely repeating things they’ve seen. But that doesn’t mean their understanding has the same shape as ours. Human concepts are developed through bodies, social relationships, and acting in the world. A model trained primarily on language has a very different route into those concepts.

So I wouldn’t put them on a single scale, with humans at the top and models somewhere below. There are areas where models exhibit remarkable breadth and flexibility, and areas where their understanding is brittle. The interesting question is what produces that difference, and what kinds of experience would make their abstractions more robust.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts humans’ embodied and social experience with models’ language-based training and notes that models can be brittle. It does not propose humans’ compositional synthesis of knowledge as an explanation for models having less deep abstract understanding.
